children: Lockheed Martin's business has been booming. Someone should tell investors.

The defense contractor on Thursday reported third-quarter earnings per share of $7.97, up about 15% year over year, from sales of $20.7 billion. Wall Street was looking for earnings per share of $7.52 from sales of $20.5 billion.
Backlog rose to a record $292 billion, up from $230 billion at the end of the second quarter.
Numbers looked solid. Guidance was raised. Lockheed now sees 2026 earnings per share of about $30.55. The midpoint of prior guidance was $30.30.

The updated number implies fourth-quarter earnings per share of about $8.20. Wall Street currently projects $8.56. That might be a small disappointment, but still implies roughly 10% earnings growth from the fourth quarter of 2025 after adjusting for last year's one-time charges.

Lockheed stock was up 6.1% in early trading at $585.62, making it the best stock in the S&P 500, according to Dow Jones Market Data. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average were down 0.7% and 0.2%, respectively.

Wall Street looked happy with the quarter. Vertical Research partners analyst Rob Stallard noted the backlog surge. Jefferies analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu called it a "beat," driven by Lockheed's missile business.

Earnings aren't the only thing boosting shares. Stock futures were down partly because of rising oil prices amid escalating tensions in the Middle East. Earnings from Tesla and Meta Platforms also failed to give stocks a boost. Both tech stocks were down in premarket trading.

What's more, the company and the Department of Defense agreed to a new F-35 framework agreement. It includes 850 new jets over 10 years and, including international customers, maintains production at 156 jets per year, among other things.
It's good news and removes some uncertainty. The F-35 is one of the most successful fighter jet programs in history and accounts for an estimated 25% of Lockheed's total revenue
Still, Lockheed's earnings were a relief. Coming into Thursday, Lockheed stock has declined about 16% since the start of the Iran War in late February.

Investors have grown increasingly concerned about defense stocks amid rising interest rates, higher inflation, an unpopular war, potential contracting reform, and a looming midterm U.S. election. Those headwinds are overcoming the tailwind of higher earnings.
Declines have left Lockheed stock trading at about 17 times earnings expected over the coming 12 months, down from 22 times in March.
